name: Complete blood count (CBC) with differential
measures: Red blood cells, hemoglobin and hematocrit
Red cell size and color indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC, RDW)
White blood cells and the five white-cell types
why: A CBC is the most-ordered blood test. It screens for anemia, infection, inflammation, bleeding problems and some blood disorders, and it is part of most routine checkups.
prep: No fasting needed. Stay hydrated and tell the lab about recent illness, as infections can temporarily change white-cell counts.
results: Each value is compared with the lab's reference range. Low hemoglobin suggests anemia; MCV helps sort iron-deficiency (small cells) from B12 or folate deficiency (large cells). High white cells often reflect infection or stress; low platelets can raise bleeding risk. Mild, isolated flags are common and are often rechecked rather than acted on.
who: Adults having a general checkup, anyone with fatigue, frequent infections, easy bruising or heavy periods.
faq: Does a CBC detect cancer?
A CBC cannot diagnose most cancers. Unusual white-cell or platelet patterns can prompt further tests for blood cancers.
Why is my MCV high?
Common causes include low B12 or folate, alcohol use, some medicines and thyroid or liver conditions.

name: Comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP-14)
measures: Liver markers: ALT, AST, ALP, bilirubin
why: The CMP gives a broad snapshot of blood sugar, kidney and liver function, fluid balance and electrolytes in one draw.
prep: Many labs ask for an 8–12 hour fast so the glucose result is a fasting value. Water is fine. Take regular medicines unless told otherwise.
results: Look at patterns rather than single values. A raised creatinine with low eGFR points to the kidneys; raised ALT and AST point to the liver. Glucose of 100–125 mg/dL fasting falls in the prediabetes range. Potassium is easily raised by a difficult draw, so a single high value is often repeated.
who: Adults wanting a routine checkup, people on medicines that affect kidneys or liver, and anyone monitoring blood pressure or diabetes.
faq: What is the difference between a CMP and a BMP?
A BMP has 8 tests (glucose, kidney markers, electrolytes and calcium). A CMP adds 6 liver and protein tests.
Can dehydration affect a CMP?
Yes. Dehydration can raise BUN, creatinine, sodium and albumin.

name: Basic metabolic panel (BMP-8)
why: A shorter version of the CMP that checks blood sugar, kidney function and electrolytes, often used to monitor blood-pressure and diuretic medicines.
prep: Fast 8–12 hours if you want a fasting glucose value. Otherwise no special preparation.
results: Creatinine and BUN track kidney filtering; electrolytes reflect fluid balance and medication effects. Abnormal potassium deserves prompt follow-up because it affects heart rhythm.
who: People taking diuretics, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and anyone wanting a lower-cost kidney and electrolyte check.
faq: Does a BMP include liver tests?
No. Choose a CMP or a hepatic function panel for liver markers.

name: Lipid panel (cholesterol test)
why: Cholesterol and triglycerides are major, modifiable risk factors for heart attack and stroke. The panel is used for screening and to monitor diet or statin treatment.
prep: Non-fasting samples are acceptable for most screening. Fast 9–12 hours (water only) if your clinician asks or if a previous triglyceride result was high.
results: Typical adult targets: total cholesterol under 200 mg/dL, LDL under 100 mg/dL (lower if you have heart disease or diabetes), HDL 40 mg/dL or more for men and 50 mg/dL or more for women, triglycerides under 150 mg/dL. Risk depends on the whole picture, including age, blood pressure, smoking and diabetes.
who: Adults from age 20, repeated every 4–6 years if normal, and more often with risk factors.
faq: Do I need to fast for a cholesterol test?
Usually not. Fasting mainly affects triglycerides. Follow your clinician's or the lab's instructions.
Is HDL always good?
Higher HDL is linked with lower risk, but raising HDL with medicine has not been shown to prevent heart disease.

name: Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c)
measures: Percentage of hemoglobin with glucose attached, reflecting average blood sugar over about 3 months
why: A1c screens for prediabetes and diabetes and tracks long-term blood-sugar control without fasting.
prep: No fasting needed. Tell your clinician about anemia, recent blood loss or transfusion, pregnancy or kidney disease, which can make A1c misleading.
results: Below 5.7% is in the normal range, 5.7–6.4% is the prediabetes range and 6.5% or higher is in the diabetes range (a diagnosis needs confirmation). An A1c of 7% corresponds to an average glucose of about 154 mg/dL.
who: Adults 35–70 with overweight or obesity, anyone with risk factors for diabetes, and people with diabetes (every 3–6 months).
faq: Can A1c be wrong?
Conditions that change red-cell lifespan, such as iron-deficiency anemia, hemolysis or some hemoglobin variants, can shift A1c up or down.
How often should I recheck?
Every 1–3 years if normal with risk factors, yearly in the prediabetes range, or as your clinician advises.

name: Fasting blood glucose
measures: Plasma glucose after at least 8 hours without food
why: A direct snapshot of blood sugar used to screen for prediabetes and diabetes.
prep: Fast at least 8 hours: water only, no coffee, gum or exercise beforehand. Book an early-morning draw.
results: 70–99 mg/dL is the normal fasting range, 100–125 mg/dL is the prediabetes range and 126 mg/dL or higher on two occasions is in the diabetes range. Below 70 mg/dL is low.
who: Anyone screening for diabetes, often alongside A1c.
faq: Why is my morning sugar high even though I fasted?
Early-morning hormones (the dawn phenomenon), poor sleep, stress and illness can raise fasting glucose.

name: Fasting insulin
measures: Insulin concentration after an overnight fast
why: Used with fasting glucose to estimate insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), an early sign of metabolic problems that can appear before glucose rises.
prep: Fast 8–12 hours and test on the same draw as fasting glucose.
results: Reference ranges differ between labs and there is no single agreed cut-off. HOMA-IR = fasting glucose (mg/dL) × fasting insulin (µIU/mL) ÷ 405; higher values suggest more insulin resistance. Interpret with your clinician.
who: People with a family history of diabetes, PCOS, central weight gain or fatty liver.
faq: Is fasting insulin a diagnostic test for diabetes?
No. Diabetes is diagnosed with glucose, A1c or a glucose tolerance test.

name: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
measures: TSH from the pituitary gland, which rises when the thyroid is underactive and falls when it is overactive
why: TSH is the best single screening test for thyroid problems, which can cause fatigue, weight change, hair loss, palpitations and mood changes.
prep: No fasting. If you take biotin (common in hair, skin and nail supplements), ask your clinician whether to pause it before testing; biotin can distort some thyroid results. Take thyroid medicine after the draw if you are monitoring treatment.
results: A typical adult range is about 0.5–5.0 mIU/L, though labs differ. High TSH suggests an underactive thyroid; low TSH suggests an overactive thyroid. Abnormal results are usually followed by free T4.
who: Adults with thyroid symptoms, people planning pregnancy, and anyone on thyroid medicine.
faq: Can illness affect TSH?
Yes. Acute illness, some medicines and recovery from illness can temporarily change TSH.

name: Thyroid panel (TSH, free T4, free T3)
why: A fuller picture of thyroid function when TSH is abnormal, symptoms persist or treatment is being adjusted.
prep: No fasting. Discuss pausing biotin with your clinician. Test at a consistent time of day if tracking over time.
results: High TSH with low free T4 indicates an underactive thyroid; low TSH with high free T4 or T3 indicates an overactive thyroid. High TSH with normal free T4 is called subclinical hypothyroidism and is often rechecked.
who: People with thyroid symptoms, an abnormal TSH, or on thyroid treatment.
faq: Do I need free T3?
Free T3 adds most value when hyperthyroidism is suspected. For underactive thyroid, TSH and free T4 are usually enough.

name: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPO)
measures: Antibodies against thyroid peroxidase, a marker of autoimmune thyroid disease
why: Helps identify Hashimoto's thyroiditis, the most common cause of an underactive thyroid in iodine-sufficient countries.
prep: No fasting or special preparation.
results: A positive result means autoimmune thyroid activity and a higher chance of developing hypothyroidism over time, even if TSH is currently normal. Some people with positive antibodies never develop thyroid disease.
who: People with high TSH, a family history of thyroid disease, or other autoimmune conditions.
faq: Should I retest antibodies regularly?
Usually not. Antibody levels rarely change management; TSH is what is monitored.

name: Vitamin D, 25-hydroxy
measures: 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the main circulating form that reflects vitamin D status
why: Checks for vitamin D deficiency, which affects bone health, and monitors supplementation.
prep: No fasting. If you take vitamin D, keep your routine steady for a few weeks before testing so the result reflects your usual intake.
results: Per the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: below 12 ng/mL is deficient, 12–19 ng/mL is inadequate for bone health, 20–50 ng/mL is adequate for most people and above 50 ng/mL may be too high. Some labs report nmol/L (multiply ng/mL by 2.5).
who: People with limited sun exposure, darker skin, osteoporosis, malabsorption or obesity, and those taking high-dose supplements.
faq: Should I test 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D?
Rarely. 25-hydroxy vitamin D is the correct test for vitamin D status.

name: Vitamin B12 and folate
why: Detects deficiencies that cause anemia with large red cells, tingling, numbness, memory problems and fatigue.
prep: Some labs request a 6–8 hour fast. Stop B12 or folate supplements only if your clinician asks.
results: A typical B12 range is about 160–950 pg/mL. Borderline results (roughly 200–300 pg/mL) are often checked with methylmalonic acid. Long-term metformin or acid-reducing medicines and plant-based diets raise deficiency risk.
who: Vegans and vegetarians, adults over 60, people on metformin or long-term acid reducers, and anyone with a high MCV on a CBC.
faq: Can B12 be too high?
High levels usually reflect supplements. Persistently high values without supplements can warrant follow-up.

name: Iron panel with ferritin
why: Distinguishes iron deficiency from iron overload and from anemia caused by inflammation.
prep: Book a morning draw after an overnight fast; serum iron varies through the day and after meals. Skip iron supplements for 24 hours unless told otherwise.
results: Low ferritin with low transferrin saturation indicates iron deficiency. High ferritin with high transferrin saturation (often above 45%) can suggest iron overload such as hemochromatosis. Ferritin also rises with inflammation, so it can look normal in someone who is iron deficient and unwell.
who: People with fatigue, heavy periods, restless legs, hair shedding, frequent blood donation, or a family history of hemochromatosis.
faq: Is ferritin alone enough?
Ferritin is the best single marker of iron stores, but the full panel helps when inflammation or overload is possible.

name: Ferritin
measures: Ferritin, the protein that stores iron
why: A quick, low-cost check of iron stores.
prep: No fasting required. Avoid testing during an acute illness if you can.
results: Typical ranges are about 24–336 ng/mL for men and 11–307 ng/mL for women. Low ferritin indicates depleted iron stores. High ferritin can reflect inflammation, liver disease, alcohol use or iron overload.
who: Menstruating people, endurance athletes, frequent blood donors and people with fatigue.
faq: Why is my ferritin high but iron low?
That pattern is typical of inflammation, which traps iron in storage.

name: Magnesium, serum
measures: Magnesium in the liquid part of the blood
why: Checks for low magnesium, which can cause cramps, weakness and heart-rhythm problems, especially with diuretics, acid reducers or heavy alcohol use.
prep: No special preparation.
results: A typical range is about 1.7–2.2 mg/dL. Serum magnesium can stay normal while body stores are low, so symptoms matter.
who: People on diuretics or long-term proton-pump inhibitors, with diabetes, or with muscle cramps.
faq: Is RBC magnesium better?
Red-cell magnesium is sometimes marketed as superior, but it is not a standard diagnostic test.

name: High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP)
measures: Low levels of C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation
why: Adds information about cardiovascular risk alongside cholesterol, especially when risk is borderline.
prep: Avoid testing within two weeks of an infection, injury or vaccination, which raise CRP temporarily.
results: For heart-risk assessment: under 1.0 mg/L is lower risk, 1.0–3.0 mg/L is average and above 3.0 mg/L is higher risk. Values above 10 mg/L usually reflect acute inflammation and should be repeated.
who: Adults with borderline or intermediate heart risk deciding about prevention.
faq: Is hs-CRP different from regular CRP?
It is the same protein measured with a more sensitive method that can read low levels.

name: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
measures: How fast red cells settle in a tube over one hour
why: A non-specific inflammation marker used to investigate and monitor inflammatory conditions such as polymyalgia rheumatica.
prep: No preparation needed.
results: Normal ESR rises with age and is higher in women; a common rule of thumb for the upper limit is age ÷ 2 for men and (age + 10) ÷ 2 for women, in mm/hr. A raised ESR says inflammation is present but not where or why.
who: People being evaluated for joint pain, unexplained fever or inflammatory disease.
faq: CRP or ESR?
CRP changes faster and is affected by fewer factors; ESR is useful in specific conditions. Often both are ordered.

name: Apolipoprotein B (ApoB)
measures: The number of atherogenic particles (LDL, VLDL, IDL and Lp(a)) carrying cholesterol
why: ApoB counts the particles that drive plaque build-up and can reveal risk that LDL cholesterol alone misses, especially with high triglycerides, diabetes or metabolic syndrome.
prep: No fasting required.
results: An ApoB of 130 mg/dL or higher is treated as a risk-enhancing factor in US guidelines. Many lipid specialists aim much lower for people at high risk. Interpret with your full lipid panel.
who: People with a family history of early heart disease, high triglycerides, diabetes or borderline LDL.
faq: Is ApoB better than LDL?
They usually agree. When they disagree, ApoB tends to predict risk more accurately.

name: Lipoprotein(a), Lp(a)
measures: Lipoprotein(a), a mostly inherited cholesterol-carrying particle
why: High Lp(a) is a genetic risk factor for heart attack, stroke and aortic valve disease that a standard lipid panel does not show. Levels are largely set at birth, so many experts suggest testing once in adulthood.
prep: No preparation needed.
results: US guidelines treat 50 mg/dL or higher (or 125 nmol/L or higher) as a risk-enhancing factor. Units are not interchangeable, so check which one your report uses.
who: Every adult once, and especially those with personal or family history of early heart disease.
faq: Can diet lower Lp(a)?
Lifestyle has little effect on Lp(a). Managing other risk factors, such as LDL and blood pressure, becomes more important.

name: Uric acid
why: Evaluates gout risk, kidney stones and monitoring of urate-lowering treatment.
prep: Some labs request a 4-hour fast. Avoid heavy alcohol and very high-purine meals the day before.
results: Typical ranges are about 4.0–8.5 mg/dL for men and 2.7–7.3 mg/dL for women. Urate can crystallize above about 6.8 mg/dL; people treated for gout usually aim below 6 mg/dL.
who: People with joint flares, kidney stones or metabolic syndrome.
faq: Can uric acid be normal during a gout attack?
Yes. Levels can fall during a flare, so retesting a few weeks later is common.

name: Creatinine with eGFR
measures: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), calculated from creatinine, age and sex
why: The standard blood test for kidney function, used for screening and for monitoring medicines that affect the kidneys.
prep: Avoid heavy exercise and large servings of cooked meat for 24 hours before the test; both can raise creatinine.
results: An eGFR of 90 or higher is normal. 60–89 is mildly decreased and common with age. Below 60 for three months or more is consistent with chronic kidney disease. Pair with a urine albumin test for a complete picture.
who: People with diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, a family history of kidney disease, or taking NSAIDs regularly.
faq: Why does my eGFR change between tests?
Hydration, exercise, muscle mass and diet shift creatinine, so small changes are normal.

name: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR)
measures: Albumin in urine relative to creatinine
why: Detects early kidney damage, often before eGFR falls.
prep: A first-morning urine sample is preferred. Avoid heavy exercise for 24 hours; fever and urinary infection can raise results.
results: Below 30 mg/g is normal, 30–300 mg/g is moderately increased and above 300 mg/g is severely increased. Two of three samples over 3–6 months are needed to confirm.
who: Everyone with diabetes or high blood pressure, at least yearly.
faq: Is this the same as protein on a urinalysis dipstick?
No. UACR is more sensitive and picks up smaller amounts of albumin.

name: Hepatic function panel (liver panel)
why: Screens for liver inflammation, fatty liver, bile-duct problems and medicine side effects.
prep: Avoid alcohol for 24 hours and strenuous exercise for 48 hours, which can raise AST. Fasting is sometimes requested.
results: Typical ranges are about 4–36 U/L for ALT and 8–33 U/L for AST, though labs vary. Mild ALT rises are common with fatty liver. A raised ALP with bilirubin points toward the bile ducts. Patterns and trends matter more than one value.
who: People who drink alcohol regularly, take medicines processed by the liver, have obesity or diabetes, or have hepatitis risk.
faq: What causes slightly high liver enzymes?
Fatty liver, alcohol, medicines, recent hard exercise and viral hepatitis are common causes.

name: Testosterone, total and free
measures: Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) in some panels
why: Evaluates low testosterone in men, excess androgens in women (such as PCOS) and monitoring of hormone therapy.
prep: Book a draw between about 7 and 10 a.m., when levels peak. Endocrine guidelines recommend a fasting morning sample and confirming a low result with a second test.
results: Typical adult male range is about 300–1,000 ng/dL and adult female about 15–70 ng/dL. One low reading is not a diagnosis; symptoms and a repeat morning test are required.
who: Men with low libido, fatigue or loss of muscle; women with irregular periods, acne or excess hair growth.
faq: Why was my afternoon result low?
Testosterone can be 20–30% lower later in the day. Retest in the morning.

name: Estradiol (E2)
measures: Estradiol, the main estrogen in people who menstruate
why: Used to assess menstrual and fertility problems, menopause transition and hormone therapy.
prep: Timing matters: for cycle evaluation, test on the day your clinician specifies (often day 2–5 of the cycle).
results: Ranges vary widely across the menstrual cycle, pregnancy and menopause, so always read results against the cycle phase listed on your report.
who: People with irregular cycles, fertility concerns, menopause symptoms, or on estrogen therapy.
faq: Does estradiol confirm menopause?
No single hormone test confirms menopause; it is defined by 12 months without a period.

name: Cortisol, morning
measures: Serum cortisol, usually drawn between 7 and 9 a.m.
why: Screens for adrenal insufficiency (low cortisol) or helps evaluate cortisol excess together with other tests.
prep: Test in the early morning. Tell the lab about steroid medicines, including creams and inhalers, and birth control pills, which raise total cortisol.
results: Morning cortisol is highest; a very low morning value can suggest adrenal insufficiency and needs follow-up. One morning value cannot diagnose Cushing's syndrome.
who: People with unexplained fatigue, low blood pressure, weight loss or recent steroid use, under clinical guidance.
faq: Is 'adrenal fatigue' measured by this test?
'Adrenal fatigue' is not a recognized medical diagnosis. This test looks for true adrenal disorders.

name: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
measures: Total PSA, a protein made by the prostate
why: Part of prostate cancer screening. For men 55–69, the US Preventive Services Task Force recommends an individual decision after discussing benefits and harms with a clinician.
prep: Avoid ejaculation for 48 hours and vigorous cycling for a day before testing. Test before, not after, a prostate exam.
results: Many labs flag values above 4.0 ng/mL, but PSA rises with age, prostate enlargement and infection. A raised PSA leads to repeat testing or further evaluation, not an automatic diagnosis.
who: Men 55–69 after a shared decision, and men with higher risk (Black men, family history) earlier.
faq: Can a urinary infection raise PSA?
Yes. Infection or inflammation can raise PSA for weeks.

name: hCG pregnancy blood test
measures: Human chorionic gonadotropin, the pregnancy hormone
why: Confirms pregnancy earlier and more precisely than urine tests; quantitative results can be tracked over days.
prep: No preparation needed.
results: hCG becomes detectable in blood roughly 10–11 days after conception and roughly doubles every 2–3 days in early pregnancy. A single value says little about how a pregnancy is progressing; trends matter.
who: People who want early confirmation or tracking of a pregnancy.
faq: Why is a blood test more sensitive than a home urine test?
Blood tests detect lower hCG levels and give a number rather than a yes or no.

name: STI panel (sexual health screening)
measures: Chlamydia and gonorrhea (urine or swab NAAT)
Hepatitis B and C in larger panels
why: Many sexually transmitted infections cause no symptoms. Regular screening catches infections early, when treatment is simplest.
prep: For urine tests, don't urinate for at least 1 hour beforehand. Testing too soon after an exposure can miss an infection; window periods range from about 2 weeks for chlamydia and gonorrhea to 6 weeks or more for HIV, syphilis and hepatitis.
results: Positive results need treatment and, for some infections, partner notification. Many direct-access services include a clinician consult for positive results.
who: Sexually active adults with new or multiple partners, and anyone with symptoms or a partner's positive result.
faq: How soon after exposure should I test?
For chlamydia and gonorrhea, about 2 weeks; for HIV with a lab antigen/antibody test, 18–45 days; repeat later if the first test was early.
Do at-home kits work?
Kits processed by CLIA-certified labs use the same lab methods. Collection technique matters, so follow instructions closely.

name: HIV-1/2 antigen and antibody test
why: The CDC recommends everyone aged 13–64 be tested for HIV at least once, and more often with ongoing risk.
prep: No preparation. The lab antigen/antibody test can usually detect HIV 18–45 days after exposure.
results: A reactive result is confirmed with a follow-up test before a diagnosis is made. A negative result inside the window period should be repeated.
who: All adults at least once; people with new partners, injection drug use or a partner living with HIV more often.
faq: What about PrEP?
People taking or starting PrEP need regular HIV testing; ask a clinician or sexual-health service.

name: Hepatitis C antibody with reflex
measures: Antibodies to hepatitis C virus, with RNA testing if positive (reflex)
why: The CDC recommends hepatitis C screening at least once for all adults 18 and older. Most infections are curable with 8–12 weeks of tablets.
prep: No preparation needed.
results: A positive antibody means past or current infection; an RNA test shows whether the virus is active. Antibodies may take 8–11 weeks after exposure to appear.
who: All adults once; people who have injected drugs, received blood before 1992, or have abnormal liver tests.
faq: If I was cured, will the antibody stay positive?
Usually yes. RNA testing is used to check for reinfection.

name: Urinalysis
why: A quick screen for urinary infection, kidney disease and diabetes.
prep: Provide a clean-catch, midstream sample, ideally first thing in the morning. Menstruation can add blood to the sample.
results: Nitrite and white cells suggest infection. Protein can indicate kidney stress. Trace findings are common and often repeated.
who: People with urinary symptoms or as part of a routine checkup.
faq: Can a urinalysis detect STIs?
A standard urinalysis cannot. Specific NAAT urine tests detect chlamydia and gonorrhea.

name: Prothrombin time (PT/INR)
measures: How long blood takes to clot, standardized as the INR
why: Monitors warfarin therapy and checks clotting before procedures or in liver disease.
prep: Take warfarin as usual and tell the lab your dose and timing. Big changes in vitamin K intake (leafy greens) affect results.
results: For people not taking blood thinners, INR is usually about 1.0. Most warfarin users aim for 2.0–3.0, though targets vary by condition.
who: People on warfarin, with liver disease, or before surgery.
faq: Do newer blood thinners need INR checks?
Apixaban, rivaroxaban and dabigatran do not require routine INR monitoring.

name: Celiac disease screen (tTG-IgA with total IgA)
measures: Total IgA (to rule out IgA deficiency, which can cause a false negative)
why: Screens for celiac disease, an autoimmune reaction to gluten that can cause digestive symptoms, anemia and fatigue.
prep: Keep eating gluten daily for several weeks before testing. Going gluten-free first can produce a false negative.
results: A positive tTG-IgA strongly suggests celiac disease; diagnosis is usually confirmed with an intestinal biopsy. Low total IgA means a different antibody test is needed.
who: People with chronic bloating, diarrhea, iron-deficiency anemia or a close relative with celiac disease.
faq: Is this a food sensitivity test?
No. It tests for an autoimmune disease. IgG food-sensitivity tests are not recommended for diagnosis.

name: Allergy blood test (specific IgE)
measures: IgE antibodies to specific foods, pollens, molds, dust mites or animals
why: Identifies sensitization to suspected allergens when skin testing isn't practical.
prep: No fasting. Antihistamines do not affect blood IgE tests.
results: A positive specific IgE shows sensitization, not necessarily a true allergy. Results must be matched to symptoms; large untargeted food panels often produce misleading positives.
who: People with suspected allergies, ideally with a clinician choosing which allergens to test.
faq: Can I eat a food that tested positive?
Don't start or stop foods based only on a blood test; discuss with an allergist.

name: FIT stool test for colorectal cancer screening
why: A yearly FIT is one recommended way for average-risk adults aged 45–75 to screen for colorectal cancer.
prep: No diet or medicine changes needed. Avoid collecting during menstruation or with bleeding hemorrhoids.
results: A negative result means repeat in one year. A positive result needs a follow-up colonoscopy; most positives are not cancer, but skipping the colonoscopy defeats the purpose of screening.
who: Average-risk adults 45–75. People with symptoms or a strong family history need a clinician-directed plan.
faq: FIT or colonoscopy?
Both are recommended options. FIT is yearly and non-invasive; colonoscopy is every 10 years when normal.
